docs.title: Local LLM Manager
docs.text: A small web dashboard to run local LLMs on your own machines – an NVIDIA DGX Spark, a Mac with Apple silicon, or any Linux box – from any browser on your network.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
• You want your best model recipes in one place, across the broad inference engines - vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, MLX and TensorFold (experimental) - each one start-ready with a single click.
  • You don't want to deal with Docker or shell scripts: paste one of the example recipes, download the model in the Weights tab, press Start.
  • You run LLMs on different machines - a DGX Spark, a Mac, a Linux PC - and want one dashboard for all.
  • Some of your machines have little disk space: see which model is where and how big it is, and copy models only to the machines that need them.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• All the broad inference engines. vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, MLX and TensorFold (experimental) have presets; any other Docker image or native binary works as Custom. → Recipes
  • Recipes from YAML or a shell script. Paste a short YAML recipe or the docker run / start script you already have into ＋ Add recipe - no forms. Export any recipe as YAML and import it on another machine or another manager. → Recipes
  • Weights management. One table shows which model is where on every machine. Download from Hugging Face once, then copy host to host over your network (SHA-256 checked, resumable). Recipes use {weights}, so they run on any host without edits. → Weights
  • Hub and agents. Start the hub, install agents on your other machines, and connect them with a token - or let them ask to join and approve them by comparing a join code. → Several machines
  • Hosts at a glance. A graph of the hub and every agent PC with memory, GPU and CPU temperature, what runs where, and live tokens/s, requests and KV-cache use per model. → Several machines
  • Start, stop, restart or "switch to" a model - switching stops the other models on that machine and frees memory first - plus live status, logs and schedules.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Quick start

    Install the manager on one machine, log in and start your first model.

  • Recipes

    Add recipes by pasting YAML or a script, and move them between machines and managers.

  • Weights

    Find, download and copy model weights to every machine.

  • Several machines

    Add more machines as agents and control them all from one dashboard.

  • How it works

    The idea in pictures: one dashboard, all your machines, models shared between them.

  • Configuration

    Every setting in .env, with defaults.

Settings are in the Configuration reference. Schedules, security, upgrading and monitoring are in the README on GitHub for now.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
Everything is set in the .env file in the install folder (used by install.sh, install-macos.sh, run.sh and Docker Compose). Copy .env.example to .env; the installers do this for you and fill in secrets. Restart the service after changes (sudo systemctl restart local-llm-manager, or rerun the installer).

Values marked agent matter only with DGXM_MODE=agent, hub only in the default hub mode.

docs.title: Dashboard and network
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_HOST 0.0.0.0 Listen address of the dashboard / agent API. tailscale = only this machine's Tailscale IPv4 (resolved at startup; the manager refuses to start when Tailscale is not connected). DGXM_PORT 8090 Listen port. DGXM_USER admin HTTP Basic username for the dashboard. DGXM_PASSWORD (empty) Dashboard password, at least 12 characters (shorter values or change-me refuse to start). Empty = no login: the manager only answers to requests addressed by IP, localhost or a local/Tailscale name - never by an arbitrary Host header. Always set it when other machines can reach the port: the manager can start arbitrary containers. DGXM_PUBLISH_IP (empty = all interfaces) Address model ports are published on: docker run -p <ip>:<port>:… and what {bind_host} expands to in native / host-network commands. tailscale = this machine's Tailscale IPv4. DGXM_HEALTH_HOST DGXM_PUBLISH_IP, else 127.0.0.1 Host the manager probes model health endpoints on (the published port is appended). Set it when models are only reachable under a different address than the probe default.

docs.title: Modes: hub and agent
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_MODE hub hub: dashboard, database and scheduler. agent: no dashboard, no database - only the token-protected agent API, so a hub on another machine runs models here. DGXM_AGENT_TOKEN (empty) The Bearer token a hub must send to this machine's agent API; required in agent mode, at least 32 characters (openssl rand -hex 32). Enter the same value on the hub under Hosts. The token grants full control over this machine - keep it secret.

docs.title: Models and recipes
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_MODEL_DIR ~/models Directories scanned for local model folders and .gguf files (Weights tab: "Found on your hosts" and presence checks). Comma- or whitespace-separated, several allowed, searched up to three levels deep. DGXM_HF_BIN hf, else huggingface-cli Hugging Face CLI used by "Download from Hugging Face" (Weights tab); downloads go into the first DGXM_MODEL_DIR. Gated models need HF_TOKEN in this machine's .env. DGXM_PUBLIC_URL the address the dashboard is opened with Where the other machines reach this hub, e.g. http://spark1:8090 - needed to copy weights from the hub's own machine when you open the dashboard as localhost. DGXM_HUB_URL – Agent mode: ask this hub to add the machine; approve it under Hosts there when the join codes match. DGXM_AGENT_URL http://<DGXM_HOST or machine name>:<DGXM_PORT> Agent mode: the address the hub should use for this machine when it asks to join. DGXM_AGENT_NAME the machine's name Agent mode: the name it asks to be listed under. DGXM_DOCKER docker Docker binary used to run Docker recipes - e.g. point it at podman where Docker is unavailable. DGXM_DROP_CACHES_IMAGE busybox:latest Image of the throwaway container that drops the page cache (sync; echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches) when the manager itself lacks permission. DGXM_STOP_TIMEOUT 30 Seconds a stop waits for a container / process to shut down cleanly before killing it. DGXM_SEED 1 1 adds the qwen3.8 example recipe (and its weights entry) to an empty database on first start; 0 starts with none.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_DB ./data/manager.db SQLite database (recipes, hosts, events). Readable by its owner only. DGXM_PROC_DIR <db folder>/processes State and log files of native-process recipes. DGXM_RETENTION_DAYS 90 Days to keep activity-log entries and start-time measurements; pruned on startup. 0 keeps everything.

docs.title: Scheduler and monitoring
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_SCHEDULER_TICK 10 Seconds between scheduler passes (hub). DGXM_HEALTH_TICK 15 Seconds between health checks (hub): memory, GPU temperature, KV cache, failed and slow starts, unreachable hosts. DGXM_ONCE_GRACE_SECONDS 600 Grace period for one-shot schedules ("start once at 06:00") that were missed while the manager was down; older misses are skipped. DGXM_METRICS (off) 1/true/yes serves the manager's own metrics at GET /metrics in Prometheus format (uptime, request and action counts, stored recipes/hosts - no recipe or host data). GET /healthz is always available and needs no login.

docs.title: Secrets passed to recipes (no DGXM_ prefix)
docs.text:
A recipe's environment lists secret names only (one per line, e.g. HF_TOKEN, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, EINFACHLLM_API_KEY). At start the manager looks each name up in its own environment - which comes from the .env file - and passes the value into the container or native process. Values therefore never land in a recipe, the database or the dashboard; an agent card shows ✓/✗ per name for the host it runs on.

# .env on the manager's host
HF_TOKEN=hf_…                        # used by recipes that list the bare name HF_TOKEN
TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=123456:ABC…       # used by the Hermes gateway recipe, for example

Any variable name works: put the value in .env, list the name in the recipe. HF_TOKEN is the canonical example (Hugging Face downloads); see examples/hermes-agent for a real setup.

Note for containers talking to models on the host: 127.0.0.1 inside a container is the container itself. Agent recipes that call a model on the manager's host need http://host.docker.internal:<port>/v1 (or the bridge gateway 172.17.0.1) - and what the program's own config file says wins over variables passed in here (for Hermes: model.base_url in ~/.hermes/config.yaml).

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• .env.example - the starter file with the few keys that matter on first install.
  • examples/hermes-agent - LLM + agent recipes with passed-through secrets.
  • OpenAPI docs of the JSON API: http://<machine>:8090/docs.

docs.title: Health findings
docs.text: The hub checks every 15 seconds whether something needs your attention and says so where you look anyway: a chip on the recipe card with what happened, why and what usually helps; a chip on the host in the Hosts graph; a ⚠ / ✖ count on the host chip in the top bar; and an entry in Activity (filter Health). Findings only read - they never start, stop or change anything.

docs.title: Rules and thresholds
docs.text:
The thresholds are fixed. They are chosen to fit a DGX Spark as well as a Mac or a small Linux box: memory is measured as a share of the machine's total, and the KV-cache rule only fires while requests are waiting.

Rule Warning Critical Must hold for Host unreachable - an agent does not answer – always 2 min Memory almost full under 8 % of the total free under 3 % free 1 min GPU running hot - the hottest GPU of the host from 85 °C from 90 °C 3 min KV cache almost full - and requests are waiting from 85 % – 5 min Start failed - with the cause from the log – always at once Start takes unusually long - compared with the recipe's own earlier starts over 2× the median (and at least 2 min more), from 3 measured starts on – at once

A condition has to hold for the time in the last column before it becomes a finding, and it has to be gone for a minute before the finding clears. So a reading that sits on a threshold does not flap on and off, and the activity log gets one entry when a finding appears, one when it gets worse (warning → critical) and one when it is resolved.

For example, 121 GB on a DGX Spark: a warning under about 9.7 GB free, critical under about 3.6 GB. On a 16 GB laptop: under about 1.3 GB and 0.5 GB.

docs.title: Why a start failed
docs.text:
When a recipe fails, the manager reads the end of its log once and names the cause it recognises:

Shown as Typical log line CUDA out of memory torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory Not enough memory for the KV cache No available memory for the cache blocks Killed (out of memory) Killed, exit code 137 Port already in use Address already in use Model not found No such file or directory … model, failed to load model Hugging Face login needed gated repo, 401 Client Error CUDA / driver error CUDA error, no CUDA-capable device Unknown argument unrecognized arguments

The matching line is shown on the card; Logs has the full output.

docs.title: Muting
docs.text: Mute 24 h under a finding hides it for a day: it stays on the card dimmed (🔕), is not counted in the top bar or in /metrics, and writes nothing to the activity log. Click the dimmed chip to unmute it early. Mutes survive a restart of the manager.

docs.title: API and metrics
docs.text:
• GET /api/health - the active findings (muted ones included, marked) and the rules.
  • POST /api/health/mute with {"key": "<finding key>", "hours": 24}, POST /api/health/unmute with {"key": …}.
  • /api/recipes and /api/hosts carry each item's findings.
  • With DGXM_METRICS=1, /metrics has dgxm_health_findings{rule, severity} (muted ones not counted) for alerts in Prometheus / Grafana.

DGXM_HEALTH_TICK (default 15) sets the seconds between checks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Local LLM Manager is a remote control for the AI models on your own computers. You open one web page, and from there you start, stop and switch models on every machine you have.

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    you["👩‍💻 <b>You</b><br/>laptop or phone"]
    dash["🎛️ <b>Dashboard</b><br/>one web page for everything"]
    subgraph machines["Your machines"]
        direction LR
        m1["🖥️ DGX Spark<br/>runs Qwen"]
        m2["🍎 Mac Studio<br/>runs Llama"]
        m3["🖥️ Second Spark<br/>runs Mistral"]
    end
    apps["💬 <b>Your apps</b><br/>chat, coding tools, …"]

    you --> dash
    dash == "start · stop · switch" ==> machines
    apps -. "talk to the models directly" .-> machines

    classDef person fill:#f59e0b40,stroke:#d97706
    classDef hub fill:#6366f140,stroke:#6366f1
    classDef machine fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    classDef app fill:#ec489938,stroke:#db2777
    class you person
    class dash hub
    class m1,m2,m3 machine
    class apps app
  • The dashboard is the one place where you control everything. It runs on one of your machines (the hub).
  • Every other machine has a small helper installed (an agent) that does what the dashboard asks.
  • Your apps talk to the models directly. The dashboard only switches models on and off. It never sees your chats.

Only one machine?

Then the dashboard and the models live on the same computer. You don't need anything else.

docs.title: Recipes: one card per model
docs.text:
A recipe is a saved start button for one model. You set it up once; after that, starting the model is one click. Every recipe is made of three things:

flowchart LR
    w["📦 <b>The model</b><br/>e.g. Qwen 32B"]
    e["⚙️ <b>The engine</b><br/>e.g. vLLM"]
    h["🖥️ <b>The machine</b><br/>e.g. DGX Spark"]
    r(["🃏 <b>Recipe card</b><br/>Qwen 32B on the Spark<br/>▶️ Start"])
    w --> r
    e --> r
    h --> r

    classDef part fill:#6366f126,stroke:#6366f1
    classDef card fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    class w,e,h part
    class r card

In the dashboard every recipe is a card - here grouped by machine, with a running agent on top:

You will soon have many recipes: one model in two sizes, the same model on several machines, a fast model for coding and a big one for hard questions. That is fine. Each card is independent, and Switch to makes sure only the right ones run.

Keep the list tidy

Pin the recipes you use daily, give cards a colour or tags (e.g. coding, chat), and use the host filter at the top to see one machine at a time.

docs.title: Which engine should I pick?
docs.text:
The engine (called framework in the recipe) is the program that runs the model. Several exist because they suit different machines and model files. You don't need to know them all, just use the first row that fits:

Your situation Pick Why 🍎 A Mac with Apple silicon MLX Made for Apple chips 📄 The model is one .gguf file llama.cpp Small and simple, made for GGUF 👥 Several people or tools use the model at once vLLM (or SGLang) Fastest with many users at the same time 👤 Just you, on a Linux / NVIDIA machine vLLM or llama.cpp Both are fine

Everything else (TensorFold, experimental, and Custom) is for special cases: a program not in the list, or a start script you already have. 📋 Import turns such a script into a recipe for you.

docs.title: The easy way: copy what already works
docs.text:
You rarely fill in a recipe by hand. ⧉ Duplicate takes a recipe that already runs and makes a copy for another model. Everything else (engine, settings, port) stays the same:

flowchart LR
    a["✅ A recipe that works<br/>Qwen 32B · vLLM"]
    b["📦 Another model<br/>Llama 70B"]
    c(["🃏 New recipe<br/>Llama 70B · vLLM<br/>same settings"])
    a -- "settings" --> c
    b -- "model" --> c

    classDef old fill:#6366f126,stroke:#6366f1
    classDef new fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    class a,b old
    class c new

On the same machine, the new recipe even gets the same port, so your apps don't need any change: just Switch to the other model.

docs.title: Switching to another model
docs.text:
Most machines only have memory for one big model at a time. Switch to takes care of everything in one click:

flowchart LR
    a(["👆 <b>Switch to</b>"]) --> b["⏹️ Stop the others<br/>and free memory"]
    b --> c["▶️ Start<br/>the new model"]
    c --> f(["✅ Ready"])

    classDef step fill:#6366f126,stroke:#6366f1
    classDef go fill:#f59e0b40,stroke:#d97706
    classDef done fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    class b,c step
    class a go
    class f done

The card shows each step live. When it turns Ready, your apps can use the new model. You can close the browser at any point: the machine carries on by itself.

Let it happen on a schedule

Coding model during the day, a big reasoning model at night: under Schedules the dashboard switches for you at set times, even when nobody has it open.

docs.title: Adding a new machine
docs.text:
• 1️⃣ Install

    Install the manager on the new machine and tell it where the dashboard is.

  • 2️⃣ Compare the code

    The machine shows a short code, e.g. K7Q2-X9PM. The dashboard shows a code too.

  • 3️⃣ Add it

    Same code on both? Click Codes match – add. Done ✅

The code works like the pairing code of a Bluetooth headset. If the two codes are the same, it is really your machine. If they differ, click Reject. The step by step guide is in Several machines.

docs.title: Getting a model onto every machine
docs.text:
Models are big: often 20 to 200 GB. The manager downloads a model from the internet once, and then the machines pass it on to each other over your own network, which is much faster.

flowchart LR
    net["☁️ Hugging Face<br/>(internet)"]
    s1["🖥️ Spark 1"]
    s2["🖥️ Spark 2"]
    s3["🖥️ Spark 3"]
    s4["🖥️ Spark 4"]
    s5["🖥️ Spark 5"]

    net == "download once" ==> s1
    s1 -- "copy" --> s2
    s1 -- "copy" --> s3
    s2 -- "copy" --> s4
    s1 -- "copy" --> s5

    classDef cloud fill:#f59e0b40,stroke:#d97706
    classDef machine fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    class net cloud
    class s1,s2,s3,s4,s5 machine

Like a snowball, every machine that is finished helps the next one. Five machines are done in three rounds instead of five. Every file is checked on arrival, an interrupted copy continues where it stopped, and a progress panel shows how long it will take.

docs.title: One setup for the whole team
docs.text:
Example: everyone on the team has their own DGX Spark. Set the model up once and roll it out:

flowchart TB
    o["⭐ Your setup<br/>Qwen 32B"]
    c1["👤 Anna's Spark<br/>✓ up to date"]
    c2["👤 Ben's Spark<br/>✓ up to date"]
    c3["👤 Chris's Spark<br/>⟳ needs update"]
    o --> c1 & c2 & c3

    classDef main fill:#f59e0b40,stroke:#d97706
    classDef ok fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    classDef todo fill:#f9731640,stroke:#ea580c
    class o main
    class c1,c2 ok
    class c3 todo

Everyone gets the same model at the same address. If you change the original later (a newer version, other settings), the dashboard offers to update all copies and restart them.

docs.title: Is it safe?
docs.text:
• 🏠 Stays at home

    Everything runs on your own machines. Your prompts and answers never leave them.

  • 🔑 Password protected

    The dashboard needs a password. Machines only obey the dashboard they were added to.

  • 🔒 Private network

    With Tailscale all traffic is encrypted, and it also works from your phone when you are away.

  • ✅ Checked copies

    Every model file copied between machines is checked, so a broken download cannot start a model.

Want the details?

Several machines lists which machine talks to which and on which port; Configuration lists every setting.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: This page sets up the manager on one machine and starts a first model. For more machines, continue with Several machines afterwards.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • For Docker recipes: Docker, usable by your user without sudo, with the NVIDIA container runtime for GPUs.
  • Disk space for the model weights. The manager can pull Docker images and download weights from Hugging Face for you (Weights), or you put them on the machine yourself.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
LinuxmacOSDocker Compose

Installs a systemd service that runs as your user.

git clone https://github.com/einfachllm/local-llm-manager.git
cd local-llm-manager
./install.sh

The installer prints a generated password and stores it in .env in this folder.

Installs a launchd agent. Docker on a Mac cannot use the GPU, so use native recipes (framework Custom (native)) with e.g. MLX (pip install mlx-lm) or llama.cpp (brew install llama.cpp). For importing start scripts, also run brew install bash.

git clone https://github.com/einfachllm/local-llm-manager.git
cd local-llm-manager
./install-macos.sh

The installer prints a generated password and stores it in .env.

Linux only, and only for Docker recipes. Uses the image ghcr.io/einfachllm/local-llm-manager:latest (amd64 and arm64).

git clone https://github.com/einfachllm/local-llm-manager.git
cd local-llm-manager
cp .env.example .env

Set DGXM_PASSWORD in .env (at least 12 characters, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 18), then:

docker compose up -d

Add --build to build the image yourself.

docs.title: 2. Log in
docs.text:
Open http://<machine>:8090 in a browser and log in as admin with the password from the installer (or the one you set in .env).

To change the password, edit DGXM_PASSWORD in .env (at least 12 characters, no well-known passwords) and restart the service.

docs.title: 3. Start your first model
docs.text:
1. Click ＋ Add recipe (shortcut i).

  2. Paste a YAML recipe or a shell script / docker run command - or click YAML recipe or shell script under the box for an example to edit. A YAML recipe only lists what differs from the engine's defaults:

    name: qwen3-8b
framework: vllm          # vllm, sglang, llamacpp, mlx, …
model: Qwen/Qwen3-8B     # a Hugging Face id, or  weights: <name in the Weights tab>
port: 8101

    Scripts are checked for risky calls first; nothing in them is executed.

  3. Import, check the fields and the command preview, then Save.

  4. Click Start on the new card. The status goes from starting to loading to ready, and a running model shows its live speed, requests and KV-cache use:

A second model with the same settings: ⧉ Duplicate on the card, then change the model. In the editor, Recipe file… exports a recipe as YAML.

When the model is ready, its OpenAI-compatible API is at the endpoint shown on the card:

curl http://<machine>:<port>/v1/models

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Get model weights onto the machine (download, or register what is already there): Weights.
  • Move recipes between machines or managers, and the example recipes: Recipes.
  • Run models on more than one machine: Several machines.
  • Upgrading, uninstalling, schedules and all settings are described in the README.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Recipes save how to start a model server (vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, MLX, TensorFold or any image / native binary) as a Docker container or a native process. You can also import an existing start script, docker run command or compact JSON/YAML recipe file, and export any recipe the same way.

docs.title: Supported engines
docs.text:
Every recipe names a framework:. The preset fills in the image, start command, container port and health check, so a recipe only writes down what differs from it.

framework: Engine Runs as Default image / command Good for vllm vLLM Docker nvcr.io/nvidia/vllm:25.11-py3, vllm serve NVIDIA GPUs, DGX Spark, high throughput sglang SGLang Docker lmsysorg/sglang:spark, python3 -m sglang.launch_server NVIDIA GPUs, models that ship SGLang support first llamacpp llama.cpp server Docker ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-cuda .gguf files, smaller GPUs llamacpp-native llama.cpp server native process llama-server .gguf on a Mac or without Docker mlx MLX native process mlx_lm.server Macs with Apple silicon tensorfold TensorFold (experimental) native process tensorfold serve trying TensorFold custom / process-custom anything else Docker / native process your image or binary other servers, agents such as a Hermes gateway

vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and MLX all serve an OpenAI-compatible API at http://<host>:<port>/v1, so your apps don't care which engine runs behind the endpoint. Live stats (tokens/s, requests, KV cache) come from the server's /metrics: on by default in vLLM and TensorFold, add --enable-metrics for SGLang and --metrics for llama.cpp.

docs.title: Add a recipe: paste YAML or a shell script
docs.text:
There is no form to fill in. Click ＋ Add recipe (shortcut i) and paste one of:

YAML recipeShell script / docker run

Only what differs from the engine's defaults - the framework preset fills in the rest:

name: qwen3-8b
framework: vllm          # vllm, sglang, llamacpp, mlx, tensorfold, custom, …
model: Qwen/Qwen3-8B     # a Hugging Face id - or  weights: <row in the Weights tab>
port: 8101
args: --max-model-len 32768 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8

The start script you already use - a plain docker run …, or a script that computes values first:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Flint served by SGLang      <- the first comment line becomes the description
docker run -d --gpus all -p 30000:30000 \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  lmsysorg/sglang:spark \
  python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path RecursiveSI/flint --port 30000

The script is checked for risky lines first, then run with bash in a restricted mode in which only a fake docker (that records the command) and read-only text tools really run. Nothing is started.

Under the box, YAML recipe and shell script insert an example of each to edit. After Import the editor opens with every field filled and the exact docker run command beside it; check name, port and paths, then Save. For a variant of a recipe that already works, use ⧉ Duplicate on its card.

docs.title: Move recipes between machines and managers
docs.text:
A recipe is not tied to the machine it was written on:

You want to… Do this Run it on another host of the same dashboard Change its Host field. With {weights} the model folder follows: each host mounts its own path from the Weights tab. Run it on several hosts at once and keep them equal ⇉ on the card copies it to the hosts you tick; later changes to the original are offered to all copies, which can be restarted together. See Several machines. Take it to another installation (a colleague's hub, a test instance) or into Git In the editor, Recipe file… shows the recipe as compact YAML or JSON - Copy or Download it, and paste it into ＋ Add recipe on the other manager. Tweak a recipe as text Edit the YAML in Recipe file… and press Apply to editor; nothing is saved until you click Save.

The recipe file contains everything the container needs - image, model, ports, arguments, environment names, volumes and extra Docker flags - but no secret values: a bare HF_TOKEN line is filled from the .env of the machine that runs it. Use weights: instead of fixed paths, and the same file works on every machine that has the model.

docs.title: Importable example recipes
docs.text:
Ready-made recipes you paste into the manager instead of typing fields: click ＋ Add recipe, paste a whole file from examples/recipes, review the draft (name, port, paths) and create.

Two formats are accepted:

  • .yaml / .json - compact recipe files. The manager's own fields: image, model, ports, args, env, volumes, docker_args, command, health path, tags. Missing settings come from the framework preset, so only what differs is written down. weights: names a registered Weights-tab entry (its per-host path fills {weights}); omit model: for the usual /model mount, or set it to another path. host_port: is the port on the host (port: is shorthand for it). args, env, volumes and docker_args can be multi-line strings or lists.
  • .sh - starter scripts / docker run commands. The manager checks the script, runs it with bash in a restricted mode and turns the captured docker run into the same fields.

The current examples:

File What it is qwen38-27b.yaml Qwen3.8 27B served by vLLM - a small compact recipe with registered weights. qwen38-flash-next-fp4.yaml Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4 on an NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, SM121): b12x image, tuned flags, caches, tool calling. Compact form. nemotron-3.5-super-vl.yaml Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL with a draft model for speculative decoding; both models sit in one registered folder. hermes-agent-docker.yaml A Hermes Agent gateway as an agent recipe: its own port and data volume, no model or GPU. embeddinggemma-2-llamacpp.yaml EmbeddingGemma 2 (GGUF) as an OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings server via llama.cpp. sglang-flint.sh RecursiveSI/flint served natively by SGLang's sglang serve CLI, port 30000. sglang-flint-docker.sh The same model in the official lmsysorg/sglang Docker image (python3 -m sglang.launch_server).

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Weights: compact recipes name a registered entry (weights:). Create it in the Weights tab with the folder on each host that runs the recipe, or change the name in the file. If a main model and a draft model share a folder, register that folder once, mount it, and point model: at the subfolder (see nemotron-3.5-super-vl.yaml). Starter scripts mount a concrete folder; download the model there, or point the volume at your copy. The Weights tab finds model folders under DGXM_MODEL_DIR by itself and offers them under "Found on your hosts".
  • Ports: the port in host_port: / port: / --port becomes the recipe's port. Keep it the same across models you want to switch between, and give each --served-model-name a stable short name - then Switch to changes the model and your agents keep the same endpoint http://<host>:<port>/v1.
  • Secrets: files list only bare names (e.g. HF_TOKEN); put the values in the manager's .env (see Configuration).
  • vLLM images: the preset command starts with vllm serve. For vllm/vllm-openai (whose entrypoint already runs vllm serve), the manager drops the duplicate; images with a plain vllm entrypoint keep serve. The preview shows the actual command.
  • Recipes are a starting point: the flags are tuned for the machine they ran on. Check --gpu-memory-utilization, --max-model-len and --max-num-seqs against your GPU's memory.

More of your own? Drop new .yaml / .json files in examples/recipes and add a row to its table - or export one from the editor with Recipe file….

docs.title: Several machines
docs.text:
One installation is the hub: it serves the dashboard and stores recipes, schedules and the activity log. Every other machine runs the same app as an agent, which only carries out what the hub tells it to. Only two things go the other way: an agent can ask the hub to add it, and machines copy weights straight from each other once the hub has arranged it.

 your browser ──:8090──▶  HUB (dashboard, recipes, schedules)
                           │
                           ├──:8090──▶  AGENT  e.g. Mac Studio
                           └──:8090──▶  AGENT  e.g. second Spark

 apps using a model ──recipe port, e.g. :8100──▶  the machine running it

docs.title: Hub and agents in short
docs.text:
Hub Agent Runs the dashboard, the database (recipes, weights, schedules, activity) only what the hub asks: start/stop, status, logs, pulls and copies .env DGXM_PASSWORD (the installer sets it) DGXM_MODE=agent, DGXM_AGENT_TOKEN (≥ 32 characters, the installer generates it), optionally DGXM_HUB_URL You open it in the browser, http://<hub>:8090 never - its start page only shows its join code

There are two ways to connect an agent, both protected by the agent's token:

  • You add it on the hub: Hosts → + Add host with the agent's URL and its token.
  • It asks to join: the agent gets DGXM_HUB_URL and announces itself; the hub lists it under Asking to be added with a join code derived from its token, and you approve it when the code is the same as on the agent. The token itself never has to be typed or copied.

docs.title: Add a machine
docs.text:
1. Install the manager on the new machine as in the Quick start.

  2. In that machine's .env, uncomment these two lines and run the installer again. The installer has already filled in a random token of at least 32 characters.

    DGXM_MODE=agent
DGXM_AGENT_TOKEN=3f9c…   # generated

  3. In the hub's dashboard, open Hosts → + Add host. Enter the agent's URL (e.g. http://mac-studio:8090) and the same token.

Or let the machine ask to be added

Instead of step 3, also set DGXM_HUB_URL=http://<hub>:8090 in the new machine's .env and run the installer again. It prints a join code (e.g. K7Q2-X9PM), and the machine appears on the hub under Hosts → Asking to be added with a code. Click Codes match – add only if both codes are the same: another machine announcing the same name has a different code. Rejected machines are blocked for a week; requests nobody answers expire after an hour without news from the machine. The machine shows its code also on its start page (http://<machine>:8090) and in its log. Optional: DGXM_AGENT_URL (how the hub reaches it, default http://<its name>:8090) and DGXM_AGENT_NAME. If its address changes later, the machine tells the hub itself.

The new machine appears in the host strip at the top and in the Hosts graph. Recipes now have a Host field that decides where they run.

docs.title: The Hosts tab
docs.text:
The tab opens with a graph of your setup: the hub on top and a line to every agent PC. Each machine shows what matters at a glance:

  • online / offline, operating system and CPU architecture (e.g. Linux · aarch64);
  • a memory bar (used / total GB), GPU load and GPU and CPU temperature (the CPU value turns yellow from 85 °C, red from 95 °C);
  • what runs there: models (🧠, with their port) and agents (🤖) with a live status dot, plus the number of stopped recipes (hover for their names).

The line colour shows the connection: green for Tailscale / HTTPS, yellow for plain HTTP, red dotted for a machine that does not answer. Click a machine to edit or remove it, or a recipe to open it. On a phone the machines stack along one line.

Below the graph:

  • Host details & actions (collapsed): the host table with status, platform, memory, GPU / CPU and models, plus Stop all and Free memory (stop all models and drop the page cache) per machine.
  • Ports & endpoints: every recipe's port per host, its status, live metrics of running models (output/input tokens per second, running requests, KV-cache use) and its endpoint http://<host>:<port>/v1 with a Copy button. Recipes that share a port on one host are marked shared - only one of them can run at a time, which is exactly what Switch to uses.

Keep versions in sync

Upgrade the hub and all agents to the same version.

docs.title: The same recipe on several machines
docs.text:
E.g. a company where every employee has their own DGX Spark: set the recipe up once, then roll it out.

  1. Make sure the model is on those machines: Weights downloads it once and copies it to the others.
  2. On the recipe's card click ⇉ (Copy to other hosts) and tick the machines. For each one the dialog checks first whether the weights (Weights tab) and the Docker image are there, and whether another recipe uses the same port.
  3. Copy: every machine gets its own copy, named <recipe> · <host>, with the same settings and port - so every employee has the same endpoint http://<their-spark>:<port>/v1 and the same model name.
  4. Later, edit the original (new image, other flags) and save: the manager offers to update all copies. Running copies are listed and can be restarted right away: the hub restarts them on all machines at the same time, also if you close the browser, and a panel shows the progress per machine. Cards show ✓ in sync or ⟳ differs, with sync to catch up.

Images and weights on every machine:

  • Images: in the Images tab, ⤓ Pull… on an image runs docker pull on the machines you tick, all at once (private registries: docker login on each machine once). Details on the Weights tab: Weights.

  • Weights from Hugging Face: in the Weights tab, ⬇ Download from Hugging Face…. By default only the first ticked machine downloads; the others then copy from it over your network, so the model comes over the internet once. Needs the hf command there (pip install -U huggingface_hub); gated models need HF_TOKEN in that machine's .env.

  • Weights already on a machine (e.g. from your SSD): ⇉ Copy to other hosts… on the model's row. Machines copy straight from each other - the hub only arranges it - like a snowball: each machine that has the weights serves one copy at a time and every finished machine joins in, so 5 machines are done in 3 rounds. Every file is checked with SHA-256, files a machine already has are skipped, an interrupted copy continues where it stopped, and free disk space is checked first. The jobs panel shows GB, MB/s and the time left per machine.

The machines must reach each other at the addresses in the Hosts tab. To copy from the hub's own machine, open the dashboard by its network name (not localhost) or set DGXM_PUBLIC_URL. Use Tailscale names as addresses so copies are encrypted - the copy dialog warns about hosts reached over plain HTTP.

A copy keeps only its name, container name, host and pin; everything else follows the original. To change one copy for good, unlink it: it becomes a recipe of its own. Deleting the original unlinks its copies.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
From To Why Your browser hub, port 8090 The dashboard Hub each agent, port 8090 Start and stop models, status, logs (plain HTTP plus the token) Apps using a model the machine running it, the recipe's port (e.g. 8100) The model's API at http://<machine>:<port>/v1 Agent hub, port 8090 Only with DGXM_HUB_URL: asking to be added, reporting a changed address Agent other agents, port 8090 Copying weights (read-only share with a ticket)

Warning

Keep all of this inside one private network – ideally Tailscale, see below – and never expose these ports to the internet. Traffic between hub and agents, and between agents copying weights, is plain HTTP unless you use Tailscale or HTTPS addresses.

docs.title: Recommended: Tailscale
docs.text:
Tailscale puts all your machines and your phone into one private, encrypted network. The dashboard, the agents and the model APIs are then reachable from anywhere, but only by your own devices, and the hub-to-agent traffic is encrypted.

  1. Install Tailscale on every machine (hub and agents) and on your phone, logged in to the same tailnet.

  2. On every machine, add to its .env and restart the manager:

    DGXM_HOST=tailscale         # the manager listens only on this machine's Tailscale IP
DGXM_PUBLISH_IP=tailscale   # model ports too

  3. Add agents under Hosts → + Add host by their Tailscale name, e.g. http://mac-studio:8090.

  4. On your phone, open http://<hub-name>:8090 and use Add to Home Screen. For HTTPS, run tailscale serve --bg 8090 on the hub and open https://<hub-name>.<tailnet>.ts.net.

tailscale is resolved to the machine's Tailscale IPv4 address at start-up. If Tailscale is not up yet, the service fails and systemd or launchd retries it.

Tip

Keep DGXM_PASSWORD set anyway: your phone's browser visits other sites too.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Host shows "not reachable": check that the agent runs – on Linux systemctl status local-llm-manager, its log with journalctl -u local-llm-manager – and that the hub can reach the agent's port 8090.
  • "rejected the agent token": the token under Hosts must equal DGXM_AGENT_TOKEN in the agent's .env.
  • The service does not start after setting the token: agent tokens must be at least 32 characters.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text: Model weights are big (often 20-200 GB) and must be on the machine that runs the model. The Weights tab keeps track of where each model is on each machine, finds weights that are already there, downloads new ones from Hugging Face and copies them from machine to machine over your own network.

docs.title: One row per model, one column per host
docs.text:
The tab is a table: one row per model, one column per host.

Cell Meaning ✓ ~/models/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 23.4 GB The weights are at that path on that host. ✗ A path is set, but nothing is there (deleted, other disk not mounted, …). + set path You have not said yet where the model is on that host.

Click a cell to change the path. The same model is often in a different folder on each machine (~/models/Nemotron-VL on one Spark, /mnt/nvme/nemotron-vl on another) - that is fine, each host keeps its own path. ~ is the home directory of the machine that runs the recipe.

docs.title: Use weights in a recipe
docs.text:
In the recipe editor, pick the model under Weights and write {weights} where the path goes - picking an entry adds the usual volume {weights}:/model:ro for you; in native recipes {weights} is the model argument itself. In a YAML recipe the same is one line:

name: qwen3.8
framework: vllm
weights: Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4   # the row's name in the Weights tab
port: 8101

GGUF in a folder (llama.cpp): llama.cpp loads one .gguf file, but a Hugging Face download is a folder. When a llamacpp / llamacpp-native recipe's weights are a folder, the start picks the model file in it on that host: vision projectors (mmproj-…) are skipped and of a split model (…-00001-of-00003.gguf) the first part is used - llama.cpp loads the rest itself. If the folder holds several models (e.g. Q4_K_M and Q8_0), the start is refused with their names: set Model to one, e.g. /model/Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf (Docker) or {weights}/Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf (native).

When the recipe starts, {weights} becomes the path of the host it runs on. So moving a recipe to another host, or copying it to many, needs no edits - as long as the model has a path there. The editor shows right away whether the weights are on the selected host, and a start is refused with a clear message when they are not.

docs.title: Found on your hosts
docs.text:
You rarely type paths. When the tab opens (or on Refresh) every host looks for model folders (with a config.json or weight files) and .gguf files in its DGXM_MODEL_DIR (default ~/models, up to three levels deep) and the tab lists what it can add in the Found on your hosts box:

  • "X is also on LocalPC" - a model you already registered was found on another host: Use sets that host's path.
  • New folders / .gguf files nobody added yet: Add… creates a row.
  • Recipes that mount a folder directly (e.g. ~/models/x:/model:ro): adding them creates the row (or reuses one of the same name) and switches the recipes to {weights}.

The box is hidden when there is nothing to add. Several model folders per machine: list them in DGXM_MODEL_DIR, separated by commas.

docs.title: Download from Hugging Face
docs.text:
⬇ Download from Hugging Face… (top right, or ⬇ Download… on a model no host has yet) takes a repo id such as nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 and the hosts that should get it.

  • By default only the first ticked host downloads; the others copy from it over your network, so the model comes over the internet once.
  • Downloads go into the host's first DGXM_MODEL_DIR and the row's path is set when they finish.
  • The host needs the hf command (pip install -U huggingface_hub; set DGXM_HF_BIN for another binary). Gated models need HF_TOKEN in that host's .env.

docs.title: Copy weights to other hosts
docs.text:
A model that is on one machine already (downloaded, or copied there from your SSD) gets ⇉ Copy to other hosts… on its row. Tick the target hosts and the jobs panel shows GB, MB/s and the time left per machine.

flowchart LR
    hf["☁️ Hugging Face"]
    a["🖥️ Spark 1"]
    b["🖥️ Spark 2"]
    c["🖥️ Spark 3"]
    d["🖥️ Spark 4"]
    hf == "download once" ==> a
    a -- "round 1" --> b
    a -- "round 2" --> c
    b -- "round 2" --> d
  • Machine to machine: the hub only arranges the copy; the data goes straight from one host to the other (a read-only share protected by a one-time ticket).
  • Snowball: each host that has the weights serves one copy at a time and every finished host joins in, so 5 machines are done in 3 rounds.
  • Safe and resumable: every file is checked with SHA-256, files a host already has are skipped, an interrupted copy continues where it stopped, and free disk space is checked first.
  • Encrypted when the hosts reach each other over Tailscale or HTTPS - the dialog warns about plain HTTP addresses.

To copy from the hub's own machine, open the dashboard by its network name (not localhost) or set DGXM_PUBLIC_URL.

docs.title: Machines with little disk space
docs.text: Not every machine can hold every model. The table shows each model's size per host, so you see at a glance what fills a disk. Keep a model on one machine (or a NAS-mounted folder) and ⇉ copy it only to the machines that need it now; free disk space is checked before a copy starts. After deleting a model folder on a host, Refresh turns its cell into ✗ and recipes that use it there refuse to start with a clear message instead of failing halfway.

docs.title: Typical flow
docs.text:
1. Download from Hugging Face… onto one host - or let Found on your hosts pick up what is already on disk.
  2. ⇉ Copy to other hosts… to every machine that should run it.
  3. In the recipe pick it under Weights (weights: in YAML) and ⇉ copy the recipe to the same hosts (Several machines). Every copy finds the model at its own path.
